newsitem.title: CHINA: China stocks in for volatile ride but heading up.
newsitem.headline: China stocks in for volatile ride but heading up.

text.p: China's seesaw stock markets are in for a volatile ride over the next few weeks, with investor enthusiasm and positive fundamentals battling with officials determined to bring order to trading, analysts said on Sunday.

Over the last week, the Chinese securities authorities have indicated clearly with a series of measures and announcements that they have lost their patience with speculators pushing stocks too high, too fast.

Share markets in Shanghai and Shenzhen plummeted on Friday on the twin announcements of a massive injection of new share issues in 1887 and the suspension of four companies pending investigations into price fluctuations.

Markets are now rife with rumours that the top securities regulator, Zhou Daijiong, head of the China Securities Regulatory Commission, will soon be moved from his post for failing to control the markets properly.
And several major brokerages are said to be about to be punished for trading irregularities.

"My guess is the markets are going to be a little weak for a while, but the government doesn't want to kill the market," said an analyst with a foreign brokerage in Shanghai. "Over the medium term, the (foreign currency) B shares are heading up."
On Friday, Shanghai's B share index fell 4.332 points or 4.88 percent to 84.438 while Shenzhen's B share index fell 13.46 points or 7.8 percent to 159.07,

A local investor in the Shanghai A share market predicted the index, which finished Friday at 1,375.910, down 107.333 or 7.24 percent, would probably fall to 1,200 -- roughly a further 12 percent -- before touching bottom.
Analyst said B shares were expected to fall less than A shares and recover faster.

The brokerage analyst said the government was concerned that small investors, who are currently entering the markets in record numbers, could get caught if major players, including institutions, ramped stocks higher and then quickly sold off.
"What Beijing is concerned about is the possibility of local investors being left holding the shares after the institutions get out," he said.

The pre-emptive strike is viewed by analysts as being positive for the development of the Chinese share markets in the medium term, in spite of its dampening effect on the effervescence of recent months.
"However painful this is in the short-term, it is good for China's share markets in the long term," said another stock analyst.
Major local brokerages are expected to pull back in the coming sessions, although one analyst said small investors could buy into the falls and support prices.

The government has announced large increases in the quota for share issues, but analysts said that given the size of the Chinese economy and the amount of surplus funds in the system, the quantities so far would not swamp the markets.

"The market is still very small compared to the entire Chinese economy," said one analyst. "So even with all this extra stock coming on stream, it will be a short-term issue and good for healthy development."
